title: RAG Retrieval Tuning: Chunking, Hybrid Search, Re-ranking and Evaluation
summary: Quick revision notes on tuning the retrieval step of a RAG system. They cover chunk size and overlap, metadata filtering, hybrid search, re-ranking and query rewriting, then how to measure retrieval with recall@k and MRR.

chapters.title: Retrieval Mental Model
points: Retrieval is the step that picks the top-k chunks from an index to put in the LLM prompt. If the right chunk is not retrieved, the answer cannot be grounded, however good the model is.
Pipeline order: rewrite query, filter by metadata, retrieve candidates (dense + keyword), re-rank, take the top few chunks, generate.
Two-stage idea: stage 1 is cheap and wide (high recall, top 50-100). Stage 2 is slow and precise (re-ranker, top 3-5).
Dense vectors match meaning but miss exact tokens such as IDs, error codes and names. Keyword search (BM25) matches exact tokens but misses paraphrases.
Interview Point: Why can a RAG system hallucinate even with a strong LLM? Which stage do you debug first, retrieval or generation? Why do retrieval and generation need separate metrics?

chapters.title: Chunk Size and Overlap
points: Chunk size is how much text becomes one embedding (counted in tokens). Overlap is the share of the previous chunk repeated at the start of the next one.
Small chunks (100-200 tokens) give precise matches but lose context. Large chunks (800-1500 tokens) keep context but dilute the embedding and waste prompt space.
Common starting point: 256-512 tokens with 10-20% overlap. Tune it against recall@k on your own queries rather than trusting a default.
Overlap stops a fact being split across a chunk boundary. Example: size 500, overlap 50 means chunk 2 starts at token 450. The cost is a larger index and near-duplicate hits.

Split on structure (headings, paragraphs, code blocks) before falling back to fixed token windows. Mistakes: zero overlap, 50% overlap that duplicates the index, one chunk size for every document type. Interview Point: How do you choose a chunk size? What does overlap fix and what does it cost? Why does a bigger chunk lower retrieval precision?

chapters.title: Metadata Filtering and Hybrid Search
points: Metadata filtering restricts candidates by structured fields (source, date, tenant_id, doc type, language) before or during the vector search.
Pre-filtering applies the filter inside the ANN search and is exact. Post-filtering takes top-k first and then filters, so it can return fewer than k or zero results. Prefer pre-filtering.
Hybrid search runs BM25 and dense retrieval in parallel and merges the two ranked lists. Use it when queries contain IDs, acronyms or error codes.
Reciprocal Rank Fusion: score = sum of 1/(k+rank) across lists, with k about 60. It needs no score normalisation. The alternative is a weighted sum, which needs normalised scores.

Mistakes: filtering on fields that were never stored at ingest, using post-filtering with a selective filter, summing raw BM25 and cosine scores. Always filter by tenant_id for multi-tenant data. Interview Point: Pre-filter vs post-filter? Why is RRF preferred over adding scores? When does BM25 beat embeddings?

chapters.title: Re-ranking and Query Rewriting
points: A re-ranker rescores the retrieved candidates against the query and reorders them. Retrieve about 50, re-rank, keep the top 3-5.

A bi-encoder embeds the query and the document separately, so it is fast and can be indexed. A cross-encoder reads query and document together, so it is more accurate but too slow to run over the whole corpus.
Re-ranking only reorders what stage 1 returned. If the answer is not in the candidate set, it cannot help. Fix recall first, then precision.

Query rewriting techniques: expand abbreviations, rewrite a follow-up into a standalone question using chat history, HyDE (embed a generated hypothetical answer), and multi-query (several paraphrases, results merged).

Mistakes: re-ranking too few candidates, rewriting that drifts from the user's intent, adding latency with no measured gain. Interview Point: Bi-encoder vs cross-encoder? Why not use a cross-encoder for first-stage retrieval? When does query rewriting help in chat?

chapters.title: Measuring Retrieval: recall@k and MRR
points: Build a labelled set of (query, relevant chunk or doc IDs) pairs, ideally 50-200 real queries. Without this set, tuning is guesswork.

recall@k = share of a query's relevant chunks found in the top k, averaged over queries; with one relevant chunk per query this is the share of queries with a hit in the top k (hit rate). Example: 8 of 10 queries hit in the top 5 gives recall@5 = 0.8.
MRR = mean of 1/rank of the first relevant result. Ranks 1, 2 and 4 give (1 + 0.5 + 0.25)/3 = 0.583. It rewards putting the right chunk first.

recall@k measures candidate coverage and is the metric for stage 1. MRR (or nDCG) measures ordering and is the metric for the re-ranker. Change one variable at a time, such as chunk size or hybrid on/off, and re-measure.

Mistakes: evaluating on synthetic queries only, tuning on the test queries, reporting only the average without checking failing queries, using k larger than the prompt can hold. Interview Point: recall@k vs MRR? How would you decide between two chunk sizes? Why is end-to-end answer quality not enough?

chapters.title: Retrieval Tuning Cheat Sheet
points: Chunking: 256-512 tokens, 10-20% overlap, split on structure first. Choose the size by recall@k, not by habit.
Filtering and hybrid: pre-filter on metadata (always tenant_id). Run BM25 plus dense and merge with RRF, score = sum of 1/(60+rank).
Re-ranking: retrieve about 50 with a bi-encoder, re-score with a cross-encoder, keep the top 3-5. It cannot recover a chunk that was never retrieved.
Query rewriting: standalone follow-ups, expansion, HyDE, multi-query. Check that each rewrite improves the metrics.

Metrics: recall@k = relevant chunks in the top k / all relevant chunks, averaged over queries (equal to hit rate when each query has one relevant chunk). MRR = mean of 1/rank of the first relevant result. Debug order: recall@k first (chunking, hybrid, filters), then MRR (re-ranker).
